\chapter{Good Morning}
\label{ch:la-good-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say good morning in Latin, and describe the salūtātiō Romans actually performed at dawn.}

Say bonum māne, note that its neuter case is invisible, and describe the dawn salūtātiō Romans really used.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bonum māne]{bonum māne — a phrase Romans didn't say, and a ritual they actually did}

\label{lesson:LA-C32-bonum-mane}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{bonus} (good) and \emph{māne} (morning, last lesson). Put them together for \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} — but this time, watch for what's \textbf{missing}, not just what's uncertain.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Bonum māne} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good morning}.\textquotedblright{} Like \emph{bonam noctem} two lessons ago, this specific phrase is \textbf{not} classically attested as a fixed Roman greeting. But here the honesty runs one level deeper: \emph{bonam noctem} showed you real, solid grammar — the accusative \emph{noctem}, distinct from nominative \emph{nox}, demonstrating Latin's genuine \textquotedblleft{}Accusative of Exclamation.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Māne}, though, is \textbf{neuter} and \textbf{indeclinable} — and Latin neuter nouns \textbf{never} distinguish nominative from accusative, in any word, ever. \emph{Bonum} works identically whether you imagine it as nominative or accusative. The grammar point that made \emph{bonam noctem} interesting simply \textbf{isn't visible} here — not because it's missing, but because neuter words never show it, for anyone, anywhere in Latin.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Here's what Romans \textbf{did} have, richly documented: the \textbf{salūtātiō} (\emph{mātūtīna salūtātiō}, \textquotedblleft{}morning greeting\textquotedblright{}) — clients arriving at their patron's house at \textbf{dawn}, formally dressed, to pay respects, ask favors, and sometimes receive the \emph{sportula} (a small cash or food allowance) in return. It structured the start of the Roman day the way a verbal \textquotedblleft{}good morning\textquotedblright{} structures yours — just as a \textbf{ritual visit}, not a \textbf{spoken phrase}.

\textbf{Salūtātiō} comes from \textbf{salūtāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to greet\textquotedblright{}), which comes from \textbf{salūs} (\textquotedblleft{}health, safety, wholeness\textquotedblright{}) — and \emph{salūs} is a genuine \textbf{doublet} of \textbf{salvus} (\textquotedblleft{}safe, sound\textquotedblright{}), the very root behind \textbf{salvē} (Chapter 1's first word, \textquotedblleft{}hello,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}be well\textquotedblright{}). Both \emph{salūs} and \emph{salvus} descend from the same \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} root, \emph{\textbf{*solh\textsubscript{2}-}} (\textquotedblleft{}whole\textquotedblright{}). So Rome's real morning greeting and its very first \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{} share one root, arrived at by two separate paths — a wish for someone's wholeness, whether spoken as \emph{salvē} or enacted at dawn as the \emph{salūtātiō}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bonum māne\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} a modern phrase, not classical
  \item why its grammar is invisible — māne is neuter, and neuters never show nominative vs. accusative
  \item \textquotedblleft{}salūtātiō\textquotedblright{} — the real Roman morning greeting, a dawn visit, not a phrase — from the same root as salvē
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \emph{bonum māne} show the same accusative-of-wishing grammar that \emph{bonam noctem} did? (\textbf{No} — māne is neuter, and Latin neuters never distinguish nominative from accusative, so the case is invisible either way.) What was Rome's real, richly documented \textquotedblleft{}morning greeting\textquotedblright{}? (The \textbf{salūtātiō} — clients visiting a patron's house at dawn.) What word, already taught in Chapter 1, shares its root with salūtātiō? (\textbf{Salvē} — both salūs and salvus descend from the same PIE root, \emph{*solh\textsubscript{2}-}, \textquotedblleft{}whole.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
